newsitem.title: THAILAND: Opposition leader Chuan poised for top Thai job.
newsitem.headline: Opposition leader Chuan poised for top Thai job.

text.p: Veteran politician Chuan Leekpai, who as opposition leader helped topple the previous Thai government, is poised to regain the nation's top job in Sunday's general election after a lapse of over 16 months.

Considered the darling of the business community, which widely believes he is the only leader who can salvage Thailand's slowing economy, the former premier has wooed supporters by promising to stabilise the economy.

Although Chuan failed to complete his four-year mandate and was forced to dissolve parliament in May 1995, the leader of the Democrat Party made history by becoming the the country's longest-serving democratically-elected premier.

Chuan, a shy, soft-spoken and youthful-looking 58-year old, was ousted as prime minister after his party became embroiled in a land scandal and faced with loss of support he was forced to call fresh elections in July 1995.

Chuan's government was tarnished by the scandal. The opposition charged that a land scheme, intended to help poor farmers, was manipulated by some Democrats to benefit wealthy business associations in a southern province.
The Democrats narrowly lost to the opposition Chart Thai party led by current outgoing premier Banharn Silpa-archa in last year's election and Chuan became opposition leader.
The former lawyer was first elected premier in the September 1992 election which followed bloody pro-democracy demonstrations on Bangkok against an unpopular military-backed government.
Chuan's Democrats had narrowly beaten Chart Thai in that election and formed a fragile five-party coalition.

Political analysts and diplomats say Chuan, although not the most glamorous and decisive leader, kept Thailand's economy on a steady course of growth, appointing respected technocrats to key economic posts.
He also made inroads on some of Thailand's pressing social problems like child prostitution, AIDS and education reform.
But some analysts say Chuan was unable to accomplish all that he wanted in his 20 months as premier due partly to inter-party squabbles and changes in coalition partners.
Other critics said Chuan's cautious nature made him appear indecisive over major issues at crucial times.

Chuan told Reuters in a recent interview that one of his key goals was to rid the country of old-style money politicking. He accused other political parties of engaging in vote buying and corruption in order to win the election.
"In their attempt to get the most seats, political parties backed by some big businessmen are using lots of money to buy over MPs, regardless of quality," he said.
"There is more political awareness now against money politics, especially after what people saw happen in the last 14 months with the outgoing administration," he said.
Traditionally, millions of dollars are spent by cash-rich political parties to lure strong politicians to defect to their parties and to buy votes in elections, analysts said.
Although his administration was hit by the land scandal, Chuan is seen as a clean politician with a long and steady run in politics.
Chuan was born in southern Trang province.
He briefly practised law after graduating from Thammasat University in 1962, but then became a full-time politician in 1969 when he was elected to parliament for the first time.
Chuan has won his home province seat 10 times in a row.
